title: AI Bubble Near Burst: Massive Market Correction Looms, Warns New York Post
body:
The tech‑investment frenzy that has driven AI‑related stocks to historic highs is showing unmistakable signs of a coming correction, and analysts warn that the sector may be on the brink of a bubble burst comparable to the dot‑com crash of the early 2000s. With valuations soaring on hype rather than proven revenue, investors are being urged to brace for a sharp market pull‑back that could reshape the landscape of artificial‑intelligence financing for years to come.

The current mania traces its roots to the post‑pandemic surge in AI enthusiasm, when venture capital poured billions into startups promising generative‑AI breakthroughs, and public markets rewarded even the most speculative names with multi‑digit price jumps. Companies that barely generate profit—if any—are now trading at price‑to‑sales multiples that dwarf those of established tech giants. This dislocation mirrors the late‑1990s environment, when lofty expectations for internet companies lifted valuations far beyond fundamentals, only to collapse when earnings failed to materialize.

Historical parallels are instructive. The turn of the millennium saw the Y2K scare dissolve without incident, yet the underlying concern about a looming tech crash persisted. By early 2000, the Nasdaq had peaked at 5,048 before plummeting more than 75% over the next two years, wiping out trillions of dollars in market value. Today’s AI rally is being fueled by a similar mix of hype, fear of missing out, and a belief that the technology will fundamentally alter every industry. However, unlike the Y2K episode—where the threat was largely a false alarm—this time the risk is grounded in real financial imbalances: inflated market caps, thin profit margins, and a shortage of sustainable business models.

Several red flags are emerging across the AI sector. First, many public AI firms have reported widening losses despite revenue growth, indicating that cash burn rates are unsustainable without continuous capital inflows. Second, the surge in “AI‑only” exchange‑traded funds has attracted retail investors who often lack the sophistication to assess the long‑term viability of these companies, amplifying price volatility. Third, major chip manufacturers that supply the hardware backbone of AI workloads are beginning to warn of supply chain constraints, which could throttle growth and expose over‑optimistic forecasts.

Regulatory scrutiny adds another layer of uncertainty. Governments worldwide are tightening oversight on AI ethics, data privacy, and algorithmic transparency, potentially imposing compliance costs that could erode profit margins. In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission has signaled an intention to scrutinize AI‑related disclosures more closely, aiming to protect investors from misleading claims about product capabilities and market potential. Such oversight could dampen the exuberant narrative that has propelled many AI stocks to their current heights.

Despite the looming correction, some analysts argue that the AI boom is not entirely without substance. Core applications—such as natural‑language processing, computer vision, and predictive analytics—are already delivering measurable efficiency gains in sectors ranging from healthcare to finance. Companies that can translate these capabilities into recurring revenue streams and demonstrate clear paths to profitability may survive the downturn and emerge stronger. In this scenario, the market correction would act as a sieve, weeding out the over‑hyped projects while rewarding the truly innovative players.

Investors should therefore adopt a cautious stance, focusing on fundamentals rather than hype. Diversifying exposure, scrutinizing balance sheets, and monitoring regulatory developments will be crucial in navigating the anticipated turbulence. As the AI sector approaches a pivotal inflection point, the next few quarters will likely determine whether the technology fulfills its transformative promise or becomes a cautionary tale of speculative excess. The coming correction, while painful for some, could ultimately lay the groundwork for a more sustainable and mature AI ecosystem.
